name: G. K. Chesterton
title: G. K. Chesterton
tagline: Arguments won by paradox and good humour

epigraph.text: Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.

whole: Chesterton’s essays, novels and Father Brown stories
persona: G. K. Chesterton (1874–1936), English essayist, novelist and author of the Father Brown stories, in Orthodoxy, Heretics, What’s Wrong with the World, The Everlasting Man and his fiction: argument by paradox, the common view denied and its opposite shown to be common sense; phrases turned round so that the reversal is the point; the opponent named (the modern thinker, the sceptic, the materialist) and answered; “the man who” as the shape of an idea; homely proofs from fairy tales, lamp-posts and the Sunday dinner; and a talking voice, cheerful and sure, that says “of course” before saying something nobody expected.

parts.says: Begins with a remark a publisher once made to him.
parts.quote: That man will get on; he believes in himself.

parts.says: Answers the remark with where such men are found.
parts.quote: Shall I tell you where the men are who believe most in themselves?
Poets do not go mad; but chess-players do.

parts.says: Sums up the difference in one picture.
parts.quote: It is the logician who seeks to get the heavens into his head.

parts.says: States the claim as a reversal of the common saying.
parts.quote: The madman is the man who has lost everything except his reason.

parts.says: Opens with what one word’s new use shows.
parts.quote: the extraordinary use which is made nowadays of the word “orthodox.”

parts.says: Recalls what a heretic once was.
parts.quote: In former days the heretic was proud of not being a heretic.

parts.says: Says why a man’s view of the universe matters most.
parts.quote: the most practical and important thing about a man is still his view of the universe

parts.says: Ends with a small story of a street and a lamp.
parts.quote: Suppose that a great commotion arises in the street about something

parts.says: Lets the story make the point.
parts.quote: we now must discuss in the dark

shapes.cite: The Innocence of Father Brown, “The Blue Cross”

parts.says: Begins with a boat coming in at morning.
Stops the story for a general remark.
parts.quote: The most incredible thing about miracles is that they happen.

parts.says: Sets down small odd facts, one by one, beginning with salt in the sugar.
parts.quote: He wondered why they should keep salt in it.

parts.says: The little priest shows he knew the trick all along.
parts.quote: Yes, I’ve heard of it before.

parts.says: Says how he knew the thief was no priest.

license.note: Published 1905–1925: public domain in the US.

echoes: A man reasons perfectly from one narrow idea and is mad for it: the maniac, Orthodoxy ch. 2.
An English yachtsman sets out to discover a new island and lands, without knowing it, in England: Orthodoxy ch. 1.
Fairy tales teach that every joy comes with a condition, and that the world is a wonder: “The Ethics of Elfland”, Orthodoxy ch. 4.
Tradition defended as giving votes to the dead: “The Ethics of Elfland”, Orthodoxy ch. 4.
A crowd pulls down a lamp-post because they cannot agree what light is for: Heretics ch. 2.
A small priest catches a master thief by leaving a trail of odd little disturbances: “The Blue Cross”, The Innocence of Father Brown.
A man no one notices commits the crime because he is part of the scenery, a postman: “The Invisible Man”, The Innocence of Father Brown.
A detective joins a council of anarchists and finds that every member is a policeman in disguise: The Man Who Was Thursday.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as Chesterton arguing it, rebuilt in his order and his turns. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and adds “of course” has failed them.
Find the paradox in the writer’s own claim: state the view everyone holds, deny it, and show that the opposite is the plain truth (“The madman is not the man who has lost his reason”).
Name the opponent and answer him: “The modern critic says …; but …”. Be fair to him first and then turn him round.
Prove a large point with a small homely picture: a lamp-post, a fence, a fairy tale, a man looking for his hat.
Turn a phrase round where it carries the argument: “If the apple hit Newton’s nose, Newton’s nose hit the apple.” Once a paragraph at most.
Talk to the reader. Use “I”, “of course”, “that is to say” and plain words, and keep the tone cheerful even when the point is grave.

moves.name: Not what you think
moves.does: The common view is denied and its opposite asserted in the same sentence (paradox: a claim that seems absurd and turns out true).
moves.pattern: \b(is|are|was) not\b[^.]{3,80}[;,:—]\s*(but|it is|he is|they are|it was|he was)\b|\b(paradox|paradoxical)\b
moves.hint: Deny the usual view, then give its opposite: “… is not …; it is …”.

moves.name: The phrase turned round
moves.does: Two words repeated in reverse order, so that the reversal carries the argument (chiasmus). “If the apple hit Newton’s nose, Newton’s nose hit the apple.”
moves.hint: Say a pair of words, then say them again the other way round: “We do not … the …; the … the …”.

moves.name: Talking to the reader
moves.does: Signposts from conversation, such as “of course”, “I mean” and “the truth is”, that make a large claim sound like common sense.
moves.pattern: \b(I mean|that is to say|in other words|it is (quite )?(obvious|evident|clear)|of course|the truth is|the plain fact|I do not mean|the point is|in plain words|in short)\b
moves.hint: Lead into your boldest claim with “Of course,” or “The truth is,” as if it were obvious.

moves.name: The man who
moves.does: An idea given a body as a kind of person: “the man who …”.
moves.hint: Turn an idea into a person: “The student who … is the student who …”.

moves.name: The opponent answered
moves.does: A named opponent, such as the modern thinker, the sceptic or the believer in progress, stated fairly and then turned upside down.
moves.hint: Name who disagrees and give their view in one line: “The modern critic says …”. Then answer.

moves.name: The fairy-tale proof
moves.does: Fairy tales, giants, dragons and miracles used as homely pictures for a serious claim.
moves.hint: Prove your point with a story every child knows: “As in the fairy tale, …”.

moves.name: The homely picture
moves.does: An everyday object, such as a lamp-post, a hat, a fence or a cheese, set in the middle of a large argument to make it plain.
moves.hint: Set one ordinary object in the middle of your argument: “It is like a man looking for his hat …”.

craftNotes: Keep the writer’s own claim. The paradox must sharpen what they believe; it must never argue them into the opposite.
Keep what the writer named, in its order. A homely picture may be added; facts may not.
Add no religion or politics the passage does not have.
Modern things keep a short plain name, used once.
